ann_82.text: Across the whole model, a higher daytime charge clearly raises the predicted chance of leaving, slowly at first, then faster, and this part makes it even more so for customers with 180 daytime minutes or fewer: from about 2% to about 47%, against below 1% to about 19% above that.

Through this part itself, a higher daytime charge lowers it steadily up to about 25.73 US dollars (between 24.80 and 31.05 US dollars for different customers), where this part switches off, then no further: for the typical customer, going from 15.49 to 59.76 US dollars moves it from about 11% to about 3%, and across the usual range it slightly lowers it (on the training data only).

For the typical customer this part acts on (one with 2 customer-service calls and about 131 daytime minutes), customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it in an uneven way, from about 3% to about 6%.
This part acts on 1341 of 4000 customers, 200 of whom left; for the typical one it slightly raises the chance from about 2% to about 3%.
In Nebraska the daytime charge counts slightly more, still steadily: from below 1% to about 27% there, against about 1% to about 23% elsewhere.

For a typical customer in Alabama, calls slightly add to it from 4 calls upwards, in an uneven way, from about 3% to about 6% (the model has little data on this: 16 customers there are past that point).
